title: A1 — Data security controls
bodyMarkdown:
## Data security controls

Exam task **1.3**. Every drill for this task is built from the concepts below — read this before you attempt them. Access controls themselves (IAM, SCPs, resource policies) were covered in lesson 1.1, and network-layer and application-layer controls (security groups, NACLs, WAF, Shield, GuardDuty, Macie, Secrets Manager) were covered in lesson 1.2 — this lesson does not repeat them and instead focuses on protecting the data itself: who governs it, how it is classified and retained, how it is recovered, and how it is encrypted.

### K01 — Data access and governance

Data governance is not one service — it is the combination of controls that decide who can reach data and how that access is proven and audited. The access side reuses the identity tools from lesson 1.1: IAM identity-based policies, S3 bucket policies and other resource-based policies, and organization-wide SCPs. Governance adds a layer that keeps those controls consistent and auditable at scale, mainly through two features:

- **AWS Organizations tag policies** standardize the tag keys and values used across every account — for example, enforcing that every bucket carries a `DataClassification` tag with an approved value (`Public`, `Internal`, `Confidential`, `Restricted`) — and can enforce compliance on specified resource types, rejecting a noncompliant tagging request.
- **AWS Config** continuously evaluates resource configuration against rules (managed or custom), such as one that flags any S3 bucket without default encryption or with public read access enabled.

Neither grants or denies access by itself; both make sure the controls you already have are applied consistently and provably.

**Exam tip:** "our tagging standard for data classification keeps drifting across 40 accounts" points to an AWS Organizations tag policy, not to editing each bucket's policy by hand.

### K02 — Data recovery

Data recovery is the ability to restore data after it is lost, corrupted, or deleted — distinct from **availability**, which is about the data staying reachable while nothing has gone wrong.

**AWS Backup** is the AWS-wide recovery tool: it centralizes backup plans across many services (Amazon EBS, Amazon RDS, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon EFS, Amazon S3, and more) in one console, assigns resources to plans by tag, applies lifecycle rules that move older backups to a low-cost cold storage tier, and can copy backups to another AWS Region or another AWS account for extra durability. Restoring from an AWS Backup recovery point returns a resource (or the requested data) to the point captured in that backup — including a version from before an accidental delete or a bad write.

**Amazon S3 replication** (covered under S05) is not a backup by itself: live replication only propagates new and changed objects going forward, is asynchronous, and does not protect against something already wrong with the source object unless the destination is also versioned and isolated from the same accidental-delete action. Recovery requires an actual point-in-time copy you can restore from — a backup or an S3 version — not just a second live copy of current data.

**Exam tip:** "recover data to a point before an accidental delete" is a backup/restore or a versioned-object recovery, not live replication alone.

### K03 — Data retention and classification

**Classification** categorizes data by sensitivity and criticality (public, internal, confidential, restricted, and so on) so the right protection and retention controls get applied — see lesson 1.2 for **Amazon Macie**, which automatically discovers and classifies sensitive data inside Amazon S3.

**Retention** is how long data must be kept, and sometimes how it must be protected from deletion during that time:

- **S3 Lifecycle expiration** rules delete objects automatically past an age threshold you define — useful for "delete after N days," but anyone with delete permissions can still remove the object before that date, unless it is also locked.
- **S3 Object Lock** enforces a **write-once-read-many (WORM)** model on individual object versions: a **retention period** locks the object until a retain-until-date, and a **legal hold** locks it with no expiration until explicitly removed. In **compliance mode**, no principal — including the AWS account root user — can shorten the retention period or delete the object before it expires; **governance mode** gives the same protection but lets principals with the `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` permission override it. A Lifecycle expiration rule cannot delete a locked object version; S3 places a delete marker instead.
- **Glacier Vault Lock** is the equivalent WORM control for the older, standalone Amazon Glacier vault service (not the S3 Glacier storage classes): once locked, a Vault Lock policy can never be changed or removed. Amazon Glacier no longer accepts new customers, so current designs needing object-level WORM in S3 (including the S3 Glacier storage classes) use S3 Object Lock instead.

**Exam tip:** "must be provably undeletable, even by an administrator, for a fixed retention period" is S3 Object Lock in compliance mode (or, for the legacy standalone Glacier vault service, a locked Vault Lock policy) — not a Lifecycle rule by itself, which anyone with delete permissions can still race.

### K04 — Encryption and appropriate key management

**AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS)** is the managed service behind almost all encryption at rest on AWS. It works with three kinds of keys:

- **Customer managed keys** are created and controlled entirely by you: you set the key policy, choose whether to enable rotation, and pay a monthly fee plus a per-request fee. Use these when you need full control over who can use a key and want to audit and rotate it yourself.
- **AWS managed keys** (alias `aws/<service>`, such as `aws/s3` or `aws/ebs`) are created automatically the first time a service needs one. AWS controls the key policy (you can view it but not edit it), rotates it automatically every year, and there is no monthly fee — only a per-use fee, which some services pay on your behalf.
- **AWS owned keys** are not even visible in your account: an AWS service manages their entire lifecycle in its own account. They are free, cannot be audited or deleted by you, and are used for encryption-by-default features where convenience matters more than customer control.

**AWS KMS vs. AWS CloudHSM** is a control-versus-convenience tradeoff, not two ways to do the same thing. KMS is multi-tenant and managed: AWS operates the underlying hardware security modules (HSMs), and you interact with keys through key policies, IAM, and the KMS API. **AWS CloudHSM** gives you single-tenant, FIPS 140-2/140-3 Level 3–validated HSMs that you administer yourself — your own users (outside of IAM), your own applications against interfaces such as PKCS #11, JCE, or CNG, and AWS cannot see your key material at all. Choose CloudHSM when a workload must run directly against dedicated HSM hardware you control (migrating an on-premises PKI application, for example) or when KMS needs a customer-controlled key store; choose a KMS customer managed key for the same usage control without operating HSM infrastructure yourself. When a KMS key is backed by a customer-controlled (custom) key store, applications still call the AWS KMS API — not PKCS #11, JCE, or CNG directly against the HSMs. A CloudHSM cluster gets its redundancy and high availability from spreading its HSMs across multiple Availability Zones, and the cluster automatically load-balances cryptographic operations across every HSM it contains — a single HSM in a single Availability Zone has none of that redundancy.

**Exam tip:** "needs a dedicated, single-tenant HSM the customer administers directly" is CloudHSM; "needs customer control of a key without operating HSM hardware" is a KMS customer managed key.

### S01 — Aligning AWS technologies to meet compliance requirements

Meeting a compliance requirement (PCI DSS, HIPAA, SOC 2, GDPR, and similar) usually means combining several tools already covered in this task, each proving a different thing:

- **AWS Artifact** gives on-demand, no-cost downloads of AWS's own compliance reports (SOC, ISO, PCI) — evidence of what AWS itself is responsible for under the shared responsibility model (lesson 1.1, K05), to hand to an auditor.
- **AWS Config** rules continuously prove that your own resources stay configured the way a requirement demands (encryption enabled, public access blocked, and so on) — right now, not just at audit time.
- **AWS Organizations tag policies** (K01) keep classification and compliance-scope tags consistent, which many frameworks require for scoping an audit.
- **S3 Object Lock in compliance mode** (K03) satisfies a regulation that demands WORM storage no one, including administrators, can shorten or remove.

**Exam tip:** "get a copy of AWS's own SOC 2 report for our auditor" is AWS Artifact; "prove our S3 buckets stay encrypted going forward" is an AWS Config rule.

### S02 — Encrypting data at rest (for example, AWS KMS)

Amazon S3 gives you five ways to encrypt an object, and the right one depends on who needs to manage the key:

- **SSE-S3** (server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys) is the automatic default for every new object upload since January 2023 — AWS manages the key entirely, at no extra charge, with no configuration required.
- **SSE-KMS** (server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys) uses an AWS managed key (`aws/s3`) or a customer managed key instead. It costs more (KMS request charges) but adds a key policy you control, CloudTrail auditing of every key use, and specific permissions (`kms:GenerateDataKey` to upload, `kms:Decrypt` to download) required before anyone can access the data — even with S3 permissions already granted. Enabling an **S3 Bucket Key** on the bucket (or overriding it per request) reuses a short-lived, bucket-level data key instead of calling KMS for every object, cutting those KMS request costs by up to 99%.
- **DSSE-KMS** (dual-layer server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys) applies two independent AES-256 encryption layers — a KMS-generated data key, then a separate S3-managed key — for workloads with a compliance requirement for layered encryption. It costs more than SSE-KMS due to the extra KMS operations, and S3 Bucket Keys are not supported for it.
- **SSE-C** (server-side encryption with customer-provided keys) has S3 perform the encryption, but you supply the raw key on every request over HTTPS and S3 never stores it. You track which key encrypted which object and rotate it yourself; lose the key and the object is unrecoverable. Since April 2026, SSE-C is disabled by default on new general-purpose buckets (and on existing buckets with no SSE-C objects yet) — you must explicitly re-enable it via `PutBucketEncryption` before it works.
- **Client-side encryption** encrypts the object before it ever leaves your application, using the Amazon S3 Encryption Client. S3 (and AWS) never see the plaintext or the key — the strongest isolation of the five, at the cost of managing the whole encryption workflow yourself.

The same KMS-backed pattern extends to other stores: **Amazon EBS** and **Amazon RDS** encryption both use a KMS key (AWS managed or customer managed), and in both cases you cannot encrypt an existing unencrypted resource in place — you create an encrypted copy instead (an EBS volume from an encrypted snapshot; an RDS snapshot restored with encryption enabled). You can also turn on **EBS encryption by default**, a per-Region account setting that forces every new EBS volume and snapshot copy created in that Region to be encrypted — it has no effect on volumes or snapshots that already exist.

**Exam tip:** "must audit exactly who used the encryption key and when" points to SSE-KMS; "the storage provider must never see the key at all" points to SSE-C or, for the strongest isolation, client-side encryption — remember that a fresh general purpose bucket rejects SSE-C uploads by default since April 2026 until you explicitly re-enable it.

### S03 — Encrypting data in transit (for example, AWS Certificate Manager [ACM] using TLS)

**AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)** issues and manages public and private TLS/SSL certificates for AWS services that integrate with it, such as Elastic Load Balancing, Amazon CloudFront, and Amazon API Gateway, at no additional charge beyond the resources those services already cost. Certificates are Regional resources — a certificate used with an Application Load Balancer must be requested in the same Region as the load balancer, and a certificate used with CloudFront must be requested in **US East (N. Virginia)** regardless of where the distribution's origin lives.

ACM's biggest operational win is **managed renewal**: a certificate is eligible for automatic renewal when it was issued by ACM through DNS validation and is attached to an integrated AWS service (or has been exported). An imported third-party certificate, or one that has already expired, is never eligible for managed renewal — you must replace it yourself. For a standalone server outside AWS's integrated services (a self-managed EC2 web server, for example), ACM's ACME protocol support can automate issuance and renewal directly on that host instead. An ACME-issued certificate cannot be attached to Elastic Load Balancing, Amazon CloudFront, or Amazon API Gateway — it is only for use directly on the infrastructure outside those integrated services.

**Exam tip:** "the certificate must keep renewing itself with no manual steps" requires a DNS-validated ACM certificate attached to an integrated service — not an imported certificate, which ACM cannot renew for you.

### S04 — Implementing access policies for encryption keys

A **key policy** is the resource policy attached to a KMS key, and every KMS key must have exactly one. It works differently from most other AWS resource policies in one important way: unless the key policy explicitly contains a statement that enables IAM policies, an IAM identity-based policy that allows a KMS action has **no effect** — the key policy is the gate that must open first. (An IAM policy can still explicitly **deny** access to a key without any help from the key policy.) The default key policy created by the console does include that enabling statement, which is why customer managed keys usually behave as if IAM policies alone control them.

Key policies are also **Regional**: a key policy on a key in one Region has no effect on a key with the same alias in another Region, so a multi-Region design needs a policy (and often a separate key) per Region. Beyond the key policy and IAM policies, AWS KMS **grants** provide a way to delegate specific, often temporary, permissions on a key to another principal or AWS service programmatically, without editing the key policy itself.

**Exam tip:** "the caller's IAM policy already allows kms:Decrypt, but the call still fails" means the key policy does not allow it (or does not enable IAM policies at all) — check the key policy before assuming the IAM side is broken.

### S05 — Implementing data backups and replications

**AWS Backup** (K02) is the right tool for one policy-driven, auditable backup strategy across many AWS resource types, assigned by tag, with lifecycle transitions to cold storage and copies to other Regions or accounts.

**Amazon S3 replication** targets a different goal — a live, near-real-time copy, not a point-in-time recovery copy:

- **Live replication** (Cross-Region Replication, CRR, or Same-Region Replication, SRR) asynchronously copies new and updated objects going forward; it skips objects that existed before replication was configured.
- **S3 Batch Replication** fills that gap, replicating existing objects on demand.
- **S3 Replication Time Control (S3 RTC)** adds a service-level agreement to replicate 99.99% of new objects within 15 minutes, useful when a requirement caps replication lag.

Combine both: AWS Backup for point-in-time recoverability, S3 replication for a second live copy for low-latency reads or a Regional requirement.

**Exam tip:** "one console, one policy, across EBS/RDS/DynamoDB/S3 by tag, with a cross-Region copy" is AWS Backup; "keep every new S3 write also available in a second Region within minutes" is CRR with S3 RTC.

### S06 — Implementing policies for data access, lifecycle, and protection

Three layers work together over the life of data in Amazon S3:

- **Access** is governed by IAM identity-based policies and S3 bucket policies (resource-based), exactly as in lesson 1.1 — the same evaluation rules apply here.
- **Lifecycle** is governed by S3 Lifecycle rules: transition actions move objects to cheaper storage classes as they age, and expiration actions delete them past a defined age. A bucket policy that denies every action cannot stop a Lifecycle rule — Lifecycle actions aren't evaluated against the bucket policy the way a user's request is.
- **Protection against deletion** is governed by S3 Object Lock (K03): a retention period or legal hold blocks deletion regardless of what the bucket policy or a Lifecycle rule would otherwise allow, and bypassing governance-mode retention still needs the explicit `s3:BypassGovernanceRetention` permission and header — a legal hold ignores that bypass and must be removed on its own.

**Exam tip:** a Lifecycle rule and a bucket policy answer different questions — "will this data expire" is Lifecycle, "can this principal delete it right now" is the bucket/IAM policy, and "can it be deleted at all before this date" is Object Lock.

### S07 — Rotating encryption keys and renewing certificates

**KMS key rotation** changes only the key material, never the key's ARN, alias, or the applications that reference it — decryption still works because AWS KMS keeps every prior version of the key material and automatically selects the right one:

- **Automatic rotation** for a customer managed key generates new key material every year by default, or on a custom rotation period you set; it never rotates on demand by itself.
- **On-demand rotation** rotates the key material immediately, independent of (and without disrupting) any automatic schedule already configured.
- **AWS managed keys** rotate automatically every year, on a schedule you cannot change or disable.
- Asymmetric KMS keys, HMAC KMS keys, and keys in a custom key store are not eligible for automatic or on-demand rotation; rotating them means creating a new KMS key and switching applications or aliases to it — sometimes called manual rotation.

Key rotation never changes data already protected by the key and never re-encrypts anything — it only affects future encryption operations.

**Certificate renewal** works differently: an ACM-issued, DNS-validated public certificate attached to an integrated AWS service renews itself automatically (S03) — nothing to schedule. An imported certificate never renews automatically; you track its expiration and re-import a new one, or migrate to an ACM-issued certificate to get managed renewal.

**Exam tip:** "rotate the key without touching any application code" is automatic or on-demand KMS key rotation; "the certificate must never require someone to notice it's expiring" needs a DNS-validated ACM-issued certificate, not an imported one.

### Warnings

- Do not use the AWS root user for routine lab work.
- Stopping an instance is not teardown.
- $10 budget alerts warn; they do not stop spend.
